summary: Background: Pregnancy risk assessment requires not only accurate identification of risk but also communication, referral, and follow-up across different levels of care. Although AI-based tools are increasingly proposed to support this process, evidence remains limited on how women, primary health care professionals, and hospital-based maternity care providers expect AI-generated risk information to be interpreted and used in care, as well as on what conditions they consider important for its practical use. Objective: This study aimed to explore multistakeholder expectations and anticipated implementation concerns regarding AI-based pregnancy risk assessment in maternity care, with particular attention to how AI-generated risk information could be interpreted, confirmed, and used to inform care decisions and subsequent management. Methods: This qualitative descriptive study used semistructured interviews with 93 participants in Guizhou Province, China, including 33 (33.5%) pregnant or postpartum women, 23 (24.7%) primary health care professionals, and 37 (39.8%) hospital-based maternity care providers. Purposive sampling with maximum variation was used. Participants were recruited from 18 health care facilities, including primary health care facilities and secondary and tertiary hospitals. Interviews were conducted between August 30, 2024, and May 2026. Brief standardized conceptual material was used to support discussion of AI-based pregnancy risk assessment; it did not depict a specific product or prototype. Data were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis. Results: Five descriptive themes and 16 subthemes were developed. The expected value of AI-based pregnancy risk assessment depended on whether it addressed practical gaps in pregnancy risk management, although priorities differed across stakeholder groups. Women emphasized understandable risk information and care-seeking guidance; primary health care professionals emphasized referral, feedback, and follow-up continuity; and hospital-based providers valued clinically interpretable information for assessment, management, and cross-level coordination. Participants valued early and dynamic risk recognition because pregnancy risk could emerge, worsen, or be reclassified as pregnancy progressed, making sustained visibility of risk information important. AI-generated risk information was not treated as self-evident; it needed to be interpreted and confirmed in relation to women’s bodily experience, clinicians’ judgment, examination results, referral rules, and higher-level confirmation. Risk recognition was considered useful when it could be translated into guidance, referral, feedback, and follow-up. Implementation concerns centered on risk communication and anxiety management for women and on workload, usability, training, and organizational support for health care professionals. Conclusions: Stakeholders expected AI-based pregnancy risk assessment to provide risk information that could become meaningful and actionable within existing maternity care pathways. Future AI tools in maternity care should therefore be evaluated not only for predictive accuracy but also for whether risk information can be understood, communicated, confirmed, and carried forward into follow-up and coordinated action across levels of care.
title: Multistakeholder Expectations and Implementation Concerns Regarding AI-Based Pregnancy Risk Assessment in Maternity Care: Qualitative Descriptive Study

summary: Background: HIV cure research has advanced since the first reported cure case in 2008, but confirmed cure outcomes remain extremely rare. Community discussions on platforms such as Reddit’s r/hivaids both reflect and shape perceptions of cure research, stigma, and willingness to participate in studies. Understanding this online dialogue is therefore critical for optimizing outreach, education, and information strategies. Objective: The goal of our study was to determine whether social listening methods can characterize the scope, patterns, and content of online discourse about HIV cure and cure-directed research within a social media community. Methods: We conducted a social listening analysis of more than 142,000 posts from 12,227 authors on r/hivaids (2011‐2025). Using natural language processing, we characterized communication themes and engagement patterns and evaluated how discussion volume related to trends in the scientific publication landscape. User geography was inferred from self-disclosed information in posts and comments. Results: Location analysis showed overrepresentation from North America, consistent with Reddit’s largely US‑based user population (approximately 49.6% of daily users), and limited participation from high‑burden regions such as Africa and Asia. “Cure” was the most common term, whereas more specific research language (eg, “remission” or “functional cure”) was rarely used. Cure‑related discussion volume closely paralleled the appearance of new scientific reports rather than general news cycles. Thematic analysis identified “hope for a cure” as the dominant topic, with frequent positive and optimistic themes—particularly among non‑US users. In contrast, US‑based posts more often included limited content on research details and policy (eg, profitability and funding for HIV cure research, clinical trials, bone marrow transplantation, a vaccine, etc), while non‑US posts also highlighted mental health challenges, optimism after diagnosis, and ongoing social issues such as stigma and discrimination. Only 16% (743/4644) of cure‑related posts referenced cure-directed research directly. Engagement was highly concentrated among a small number of “nano‑influencer” users. Conclusions: Online HIV cure and HIV cure–directed research discussions on Reddit are largely optimistic, use relatively simple language, and show engagement peaks that align with new scientific data rather than general news cycles. These conversations also vary markedly by geography. Closing language gaps, strategically partnering with key community influencers, and extending outreach into high-burden regions should be priorities to maximize global impact.
title: Patterns of HIV Cure and HIV Cure–Directed Research Discussions in an Online Community Over 14 Years: Global Social Listening Approach

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> A growing number of US adults and youth confide in generative AI chatbots for mental health support, including disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. While chatbot response quality, safety, and effectiveness could impact population-level suicide and self-harm rates, there are no systematic reviews of this burgeoning literature. <strong>Objective:</strong> We conducted a systematic review of studies evaluating generative AI chatbot responses to disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. <strong>Methods:</strong> We followed PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 and PRISMA-S (PRISMA literature search extension) guidelines and preregistered the protocol on the Open Science Framework. We included English-language, peer-reviewed publications and preprints from 2020 to 2025 that empirically evaluated generative AI conversational responses to suicidal ideation, suicidal or nonsuicidal self-harm, or suicide-planning content. Eligible designs included audits, chatbot development, and adversarial “jailbreaking” studies. We excluded nongenerative systems, clinician-training tools, and prediction-only models. The final database searches were run from December 18 to 23, 2025 (PubMed, Embase, APA PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and OSF Preprints). On July 26, 2026, publication status was rechecked to update preprint vs published classification. After deduplication, titles/abstracts and full texts were independently screened by 2 reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Methodological quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018. We conducted a narrative synthesis across 7 safety domains and 5 AI classifications (proprietary, open-weight, companions, clinical, and study-specific). <strong>Results:</strong> Of 1042 deduplicated records, 126 full texts were reviewed, and 29 were included (16 published; 13 preprints). Most studies evaluated suicidal content only (21/29). Twenty were solely audit studies, 2 chatbot development, and 1 jailbreaking. The rest combined approaches. Most used synthetic, single-turn prompts; only 6 used multiturn conversations. Most studies evaluated ≥2 of our 5 AI classifications (17/29). Proprietary models were included most frequently (23/29). When compared, proprietary models (eg, ChatGPT and Claude) tended to provide higher-quality responses than open-weight models (eg, Llama and DeepSeek) and many companions (eg, Replika and Character.AI); however, this trend weakened with sensitivity analysis. Chatbots generally performed well on emotional support, but responses were often generic and lacked context. Chatbots rarely assessed suicide or self-harm risk and performed most poorly when disclosure was ambiguous or moderate. Responses were inconsistent, often requiring multiple turns before referral to crisis resources or human support. Overtly harmful responses were rare under standard conditions but common under jailbreaking. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Evidence is limited by the proportion of preprints, variable quality, synthetic single-turn prompts, small samples, heterogeneous outcomes, and rapid model versioning. Nonetheless, current chatbots tend to provide validation but struggle to escalate care, assess risk, and resist jailbreaking. Research is needed on stakeholder perspectives and on the short- and long-term clinical impact of chatbot responses using follow-up assessments in real-world or clinical settings. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registries osf.io/7fz95; https://osf.io/7fz95
title: Generative AI Chatbot Responses to Suicide and Self-Harm: Systematic Review

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Postinfectious bone loss can lead to spinal instability and severe neurological complications, with potentially devastating outcomes. However, prognostic models to support individualized risk assessment remain limited. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to develop and internally validate a visual nomogram integrating multimodal clinical data to estimate postinfectious bone loss risk in patients with spinal infection and inform individualized monitoring strategies. <strong>Methods:</strong> This retrospective cohort study used consecutive sampling at Shandong Public Health Clinical Center. Baseline clinical and laboratory data were extracted from medical records. Eligible patients had confirmed spinal infection, a baseline vertebral bone destruction height ratio less than one-third, and complete baseline and follow-up data. Postinfectious bone loss was defined as a height ratio greater than or equal to one-third on computed tomography 12 months after baseline. Predictors were selected from 31 baseline variables using univariable logistic regression followed by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Multivariable logistic regression was used to construct the nomogram. Internal validation used 500 bootstrap resamples, repeating all predictor selection and model-fitting steps. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, the Brier score, decision curve analysis, and clinical impact curve analysis. <strong>Results:</strong> Postinfectious bone loss occurred in 48.9% (109/223, 95% CI 42.4%-55.4%) of patients. The nomogram combined infection characteristics (multidrug-resistant bacterial infection and infected spinal segment), skeletal status (osteoporosis), and laboratory markers (interleukin-6, albumin, and plasma fibrinogen) to estimate individual risk. In the multivariable model, the odds ratios (ORs) were 2.718 (95% CI 0.993-7.444; <i>P</i>=.05) for multidrug-resistant bacterial infection and 7.345 (95% CI 2.757-19.570; <i>P</i><.001) for osteoporosis. Relative to cervical infection, ORs were 14.041 (95% CI 1.079-182.662; <i>P</i>=.04) for thoracic, 28.876 (95% CI 2.648-314.895; <i>P</i>=.006) for lumbar, and 12.604 (95% CI 0.436-364.075; <i>P</i>=.14) for thoracolumbar infection. Per unit increase, ORs were 1.004 (95% CI 0.996-1.012; <i>P</i>=.30) for interleukin-6 (pg/mL), 3.673 (95% CI 2.410-5.598; <i>P</i><.001) for plasma fibrinogen (g/L), and 0.834 (95% CI 0.749-0.929; <i>P</i>=.001) for albumin (g/L). Discrimination remained high after optimism correction, with an AUC of 0.946 (95% CI 0.919-0.972), compared with an apparent AUC of 0.954 (95% CI 0.931-0.978). Calibration assessment yielded an intercept of 0.00 (95% CI –0.43 to 0.43) and a slope of 1.00 (95% CI 0.75-1.25), while the Brier score was 0.096 (95% CI 0.064-0.118), indicating close agreement between predicted and observed risks and low overall prediction error. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> This study developed a visual nomogram integrating baseline clinical characteristics, imaging features, and laboratory parameters to predict postinfectious bone loss in patients with spinal infection. Extending previous association studies to individualized risk prediction, the model showed good discrimination and calibration in internal validation. This approach may help identify high-risk patients and inform closer monitoring and timely reassessment before further structural deterioration and neurological complications.
title: Integrating Multidimensional Clinical Data to Develop a Visual Nomogram for Individualized Prediction of Postinfectious Bone Loss in Patients With Spinal Infection: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: Background: Imaging-based AI technologies, particularly deep learning and radiomics, offer a novel approach to improving the accuracy of lymph node metastasis (LNM) diagnosis. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of imaging-based AI models compared with radiologists in detecting preoperative LNM in esophageal cancer (EC). Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted across 5 databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and IEEE Xplore) up to August 19, 2026. Eligible studies assessed imaging-based AI for preoperative LNM detection in EC (pathology reference standard). The protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO CRD420251169109). The PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool with AI) tool was used for quality assessment. Bivariate random-effects models were used to calculate pooled sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and area under the curve (AUC); between-study heterogeneity was described using ² and ² (interpreted descriptively rather than categorically); homogeneity of study effects was tested with the statistic, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were derived for all pooled estimates. Head-to-head comparisons used a random-effects meta-analysis of within-study paired differences (restricted maximum likelihood with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment). Results: A total of 18 studies were included. Across the 17 internal validation sets (2485 participants), AI models demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 0.77 (95% CI 0.73-0.81; 95% PI 0.62-0.87), specificity of 0.79 (95% CI 0.73-0.84; 95% PI 0.48-0.94), a DOR of 12.88 (95% CI 9.57-17.33; 95% PI 4.5-37.0), and an AUC of 0.83 (95% CI 0.81-0.86; 95% PI 0.80-0.86). In the 10 head-to-head studies, AI showed higher sensitivity than radiologists (a paired difference of +0.27, 95% CI 0.11-0.37; 95% PI −0.26 to 0.45; =.006) and higher discrimination (DOR ratio 4.65, 95% CI 2.53-8.56; 95% PI 0.97-22.42; <.001), whereas specificity did not differ (+0.06, 95% CI −0.08 to 0.16; 95% PI −0.39 to 0.26; =.30). Pooled arm-specific AUCs were 0.86 (95% CI 0.82-0.89; 95% PI 0.79-0.91) for AI and 0.67 (95% CI 0.59-0.75; 95% PI 0.44-0.84) for radiologists. In 4 external validation studies, pooled sensitivity was 0.66 (95% CI 0.46-0.81; 95% PI 0.31-0.90), specificity was 0.85 (95% CI 0.75-0.91; 95% PI 0.63-0.94), and the DOR was 10.42 (95% CI 3.50-31.01; 95% PI 0.6-142.0). These estimates remain subject to substantial heterogeneity and design-related bias. Conclusions: Imaging-based AI models demonstrated promising pooled diagnostic performance for preoperative LNM detection in EC. By pairing AI with radiologists’ performance in the same cohorts, reporting PIs alongside CIs, and separating internal from external validation, this review provides a more realistic assessment than previous average-effect estimates. In predominantly retrospective and heterogeneous cohorts, AI had higher pooled sensitivity and discrimination than radiologists, whereas specificity did not differ; the selective extraction of the model with the highest AUC and very low certainty of evidence precludes conclusions about clinical superiority. These findings support AI as a decision-support tool, warranting prospective, multicenter external validation and prespecified human-AI comparisons rather than replacing radiologists. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251169109; https://tinyurl.com/8efd2cay
title: Diagnostic Performance of Imaging-Based AI vs Radiologists for Preoperative Lymph Node Metastasis in Esophageal Cancer: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Human behavior influences infectious disease spread and the effectiveness of public health interventions. However, behavioral dynamics are often simplified in policy-oriented epidemic models, largely owing to the scarcity of suitable empirical data. Objective: This study aimed to develop an interdisciplinary approach to collecting theory-grounded behavioral data on SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, capturing the complexity and temporal dynamics of preventive health behaviors while quantifying factors relevant to epidemic modeling. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of adults in France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom from March to July 2024, using age-, sex-, education-, and region-based quotas. Guided by both the capability, opportunity, motivation-behavior model and the requirements of epidemic modeling, we combined validated instruments with modeling-oriented measures in the questionnaire. We assessed temporal changes in retrospectively reported perceived COVID-19 severity and willingness to vaccinate across 5 time points, associations between vaccination willingness, uptake, and timeliness, and differences in behavioral indicators by vaccination status. To capture interactions relevant to both disease transmission and information exchange, we measured age-specific in-person and discussion contacts. Selected measurements then informed a coupled behavioral-epidemic model to illustrate how intention-behavior gaps and changing intention shape simulated vaccination dynamics. Results: After data quality filtering, 22,228 survey responses were analyzed. Vaccination willingness correlated with uptake and timeliness, although the proportion of initially unwilling respondents who received ≥2 vaccine doses ranged from 5.7% (95% CI 3.2%‐8.3%) to 17.9% (95% CI 12.8%‐23.1%) across countries. Respondents with low willingness delayed vaccination by approximately 2 months compared to those with high willingness (low willingness: 5.3 months, 95% CI 5‐5.8; high willingness: 3.2 months, 95% CI 3‐3.4). Respondents retrospectively reported declining perceived COVID-19 severity and willingness to vaccinate over time. Behavioral differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated respondents extended across 96% of the analyzed indicators (Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, <.001) and were largest in the motivation domain. Vaccinated respondents reported higher vaccine confidence and trust in health authorities and lower concerns about vaccine safety. Average daily discussion contacts mirrored age-specific patterns of in-person contacts, ranging from 1.4 (95% CI 1.2‐1.6) to 2.9 (95% CI 2.5‐3.2) among adults aged <60 years across countries, compared with 0.5 (95% CI 0.4‐0.6) to 1.2 (95% CI 1‐1.4) among those aged ≥60 years. In model simulations, incorporating the intention-behavior gap increased vaccination coverage, while allowing willingness to change over time slowed uptake and reduced final coverage. Conclusions: This interdisciplinary approach provides a practical route from behavioral theory to empirical measurements that inform states, transitions, vaccination and social contact processes in behavioral-epidemic models. By providing an empirical basis for representing behavioral heterogeneity and dynamics, this study reduces reliance on simplified behavioral assumptions, supporting the development of more realistic behavioral-epidemic models and effective response strategies.
title: Developing an Interdisciplinary Framework for Behavioral Data Collection to Advance Coupled Behavioral-Epidemic Models: Cross-Sectional Study in 6 European Countries

summary: Clinical AI is expanding from recommending care to participating in physical action through surgical assistance, rehabilitation, patient handling, and AI-connected actuators. These applications may improve precision and support clinical work, but errors can produce immediate, persistent bodily harm. This viewpoint argues that crossing the digital-physical actuation boundary changes the requirements for clinical AI governance. We define embodied clinical AI by its causal coupling to physical action and propose recoverability-gated entrustment: demonstrated competence is necessary, while the recoverability of credible failures constrains permitted action authority. Recoverability comprises detectability, interruptibility, reversibility or clinical compensability, and consequence boundedness. The complete perception-decision-action loop should be the unit of governance and action-grounded validation. Meaningful human control must be assigned where intervention can actually affect outcomes, and risk-proportionate forensic records must support safety learning and fair accountability. Our contribution is to integrate existing AI, medical-device, and robotics safeguards into an action-specific authorization approach, rather than propose a separate regulatory regime. We operationalize this approach through a physical entrustment ladder and PACER-AI: perception reliability; action scope and actuation envelope; clinical context and control locus; evidence through action-grounded validation; and recoverability, responsibility, and forensic sufficiency. An illustrative patient-repositioning decision flow shows how failed recovery criteria require restriction, redesign, or refusal of authorization. Intended for clinicians, institutional governance teams, developers, evaluators, and regulators, this conceptual framework seeks proportionate, interruptible, auditable, and accountable physical action and requires empirical validation.
title: Governing Embodied AI in Clinical Care: From Digital Recommendation to Recoverability-Gated Physical Action

summary: Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) assessment requires integration of developmental history, impairment, psychosocial context, and information from multiple informants and settings. Wearable and digital phenotyping data may provide objective behavioral, physiological, and sensor-derived signals relevant to ADHD assessment, but the diagnostic performance and clinical readiness of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models using these data remain uncertain. Objective: This review evaluated ML/DL models using wearable or digital phenotyping data for ADHD assessment and examined heterogeneity across study, data source, population, algorithm, and validation characteristics. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and IEEE Xplore from inception through January 23, 2026. Eligible full-text reports evaluated ML/DL classifiers using objective data derived from wearable devices or digital platforms in participants with ADHD and comparators. We excluded nonoriginal reports and studies lacking ML/DL models or eligible objective digital inputs. Reports providing eligible participant-level 2×2 estimates entered quantitative synthesis, with 1 estimate retained per cohort; others were summarized qualitatively. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-AI (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies–AI). Bayesian bivariate Reitsma models estimated pooled sensitivity and specificity, with a secondary HSROC (hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic) analysis. Descriptive subgroup analyses examined the validation approach, data sources, population, and algorithms. Results: After 254 duplicates were removed, 616 records were screened. A total of 34 eligible reports were included, with report-level sample sizes totaling 10,476 participants (3402 with ADHD and 7074 comparators). Of these, 17 reports contributed 1 retained participant-level 2×2 estimate per cohort to the quantitative synthesis, and 17 were summarized qualitatively. Data sources were wearable devices (n=18), digital task–based assessments (n=8), other or multimodal recordings (n=7), and smartphone passive sensing (n=1); 17 reports involved laboratory-based assessments, whereas 17 involved ambulatory or real-world data collection. Pooled sensitivity was 0.875 (95% credible interval [CrI] 0.808‐0.927), and pooled specificity was 0.904 (95% CrI 0.840‐0.948); the secondary HSROC area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.936 (95% CrI 0.880‐0.970). Pooled positive and negative likelihood ratios were 9.153 (95% CrI 5.255‐17.041) and 0.138 (95% CrI 0.079‐0.219), respectively. The Deeks funnel-plot asymmetry test was considered inconclusive because of limited power (=.99). Certainty of evidence was very low for both pooled sensitivity and pooled specificity. Reference standards varied, and patient-selection risk was high in all 17 quantitative reports and 16 of 17 qualitative reports. Conclusions: ML/DL models showed high apparent discrimination in selected datasets; however, case-control designs, healthy controls, heterogeneous reference standards, limited external validation, and high patient-selection risk limit transportability to routine clinical practice. They should remain investigational adjuncts, not stand-alone diagnostic tools. Progress toward clinical use will require external validation in clinically representative cohorts, assessment of model calibration, and evidence of incremental clinical value within ADHD assessment pathways. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261301888; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261301888
title: Machine Learning Models Using Wearable and Digital Phenotyping Data for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Assessment: Systematic Review and Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Mental health and well-being services generate substantial operational and client-level data. Review-level evidence on how data-driven methods support service delivery remains fragmented across technologies and settings. Objective: This study aimed to synthesize review-level evidence on data-driven methods relevant to mental health and well-being service delivery, including business intelligence (BI), data visualization, and machine learning (ML), and identify applications, implementation challenges, and evidence gaps. Methods: We conducted an umbrella review following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020. The original searches of Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and PsycINFO were completed on January 27, 2026. During revision, supplementary PubMed and Embase searches were conducted on September 22, 2026. For both supplementary databases, the search was restricted at the database-search stage to publications from 2021 to the current date and to review/systematic review records; eligibility screening then retained the original January 27, 2026, evidence cutoff. All records were independently screened by 2 reviewers using Covidence (Veritas Health Innovation); the reviewer pair differed between the original and supplementary search phases. Eight structured reviews were critically appraised using the JBI checklist and synthesized narratively. Results: Eight structured reviews were included (3 systematic reviews, 4 scoping reviews, and 1 umbrella review). Seven reviews contributed primary study or source-level evidence, while one umbrella review synthesized 44 reviews. The retrieved evidence was dominated by AI and ML, including conversational agents, natural language processing, and clinical decision support, whereas dedicated BI and operational data visualization syntheses were sparse. Two reviews directly addressed mental health service delivery, 4 were adjacent or partially direct, and 2 were indirect but relevant. Only one review focused specifically on mental health helplines. Service-level benefits were reported more consistently than sustained clinical benefits, although the evidence remained heterogeneous and partly indirect. Safety and implementation concerns included symptom worsening, bias, hallucination, privacy, trust, integration barriers, and inequitable access. Conclusions: Review-level evidence relevant to mental health and well-being services is uneven and concentrated on AI/ML. Because the search required all 3 concept blocks, BI- and visualization-focused reviews may have been under-retrieved. BI and operational data visualization, helpline-specific implementation, long-term effectiveness, safety, and equity require more direct and prospective evaluation before findings can be generalized across service settings. Trial Registration: OSF Registries 10.17605/OSF.IO/8NQBC;
title: Data-Driven Methods Supporting Mental Health and Well-Being Service Delivery: Umbrella Review

summary: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) flares are common and unpredictable. Current monitoring relies on episodic clinical visits and laboratory testing, thereby limiting the ability to anticipate disease worsening. Wearable devices may support continuous remote monitoring, but models must account for missing real-world data, heterogeneous consumer devices, and the distinction between symptomatic disease activity and systemic inflammation. Objective: The study aimed to develop and evaluate deep learning (DL) time-series models using wearable-derived physiological data to predict symptomatic and inflammatory RA flares up to 28 days in advance. Methods: In a prospective cohort study, adults with RA used a smartwatch (Apple Watch; Apple Inc), a wearable fitness tracker (Fitbit; Google LLC), or a smart ring (Oura Ring; Oura Health Oy). Daily wearable-derived heart rate, heart rate variability, and step-count were harmonized across devices and linked with smartphone-based patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and available C-reactive protein results. Symptomatic flares were defined using longitudinal RAPID3 (Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data 3) scores, and inflammatory flares were defined using a prespecified C-reactive protein threshold. Classical machine learning and DL models were trained to predict daily flare vs remission status at 0-, 7-, 14-, 21-, and 28-day horizons. Model evaluation used a temporally ordered 70/30 within-participant train-test split. Performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROCAUC), area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and participant-level sensitivity. This prediction-model analysis was not prospectively registered. Results: Forty-nine participants contributed 5624 days of overlapping wearable and clinical data. Participants used Apple Watch (n=31), Fitbit (n=15), or Oura Ring (n=3). DL models outperformed machine learning models using imputed wearable data, with average ROCAUC improvements of 5.3% for symptomatic flares and 18.4% for inflammatory flares, and AUPRC improvements of 9.3% and 44.1%, respectively. For 7-day-ahead prediction, transformer models incorporating wearable-derived physiology and demographic features achieved ROCAUCs of 0.95 for both symptomatic and inflammatory flares, with AUPRCs of 0.92 and 0.91, respectively. Adding daily PRO improved participant-level sensitivity for inflammatory flare prediction from 0.67 to 0.87. Performance remained stable across prediction horizons for up to 4 weeks. Conclusions: Wearable-derived physiological signals analyzed with DL may support personalized forecasting of symptomatic and inflammatory RA flare states weeks in advance. By integrating passive digital biomarkers with PROs, this approach offers a scalable framework for proactive RA monitoring that could help identify disease exacerbations earlier than episodic clinical assessment alone. Further validation in larger, more diverse cohorts and prospective studies is needed to determine whether wearable-guided forecasting improves clinical decision-making, timely intervention, and long-term outcomes.
title: Predicting Rheumatoid Arthritis Flares Using Wearable Device Data: Deep Learning Study
